# API reference

Everything public, grouped by task. A name shown without a module (such as `flux_dev_from_tau`) is importable from `elome` directly; the others give their module (`anvil.make_transit_target` is `elome.anvil.make_transit_target`).

## Light curves: the frontend

The batman-style interface. See {doc}`../spherical/light-curves`.

### `TransitParams`

```python
TransitParams()
```

```text
Object to store the physical parameters of the transit
(attribute-compatible with batman.TransitParams).
```

### `TransitModel`

```python
TransitModel(params, t, transittype: str = 'primary', supersample_factor: int = 1, exp_time: float = 0.0, dtype=None, use_metal: bool = True, integration: str = 'supersample', n_gl: int = 7)
```

```text
Precomputes the (super)sampled time grid; ``light_curve(params)``
evaluates the model for (possibly updated) parameters, batman-style.

Args:
    params: TransitParams (validated here; values may change between
        light_curve calls, but the limb-darkening *law* and the
        transit type are fixed per model).
    t: times, same units as params.t0/per (absolute values are fine —
        computation is float64 on the CPU by default).
    transittype: "primary" or "secondary".
    supersample_factor: average this many samples over exp_time.
    exp_time: exposure time (same units as t).
    dtype: mx.float64 (default; CPU, exact) or mx.float32 (the GPU
        kernels). In float32 the times are re-centred on the host in
        float64 first, so absolute mission times are fine; over
        hundreds of orbits the float32 phase loses precision.
    integration: "supersample" (batman's rule) or "contact"
        (Gauss-Legendre on windows split at the contact times).
    n_gl: Gauss-Legendre nodes per piece for "contact".
```

### `TransitModel.light_curve`

```python
light_curve(params) -> np.ndarray
```

```text
Model flux at the times given at construction (numpy array).
```

### `TransitModel.light_curves`

```python
light_curves(params_seq) -> np.ndarray
```

```text
(n_sets, n_times) for MANY parameter sets in ONE batched call.

``light_curve`` is deliberately one-parameter-set-at-a-time, for
batman parity — and calling it in a loop is the single worst thing
a sampler can do here (a GPU dispatch costs ~0.2-0.7 ms whatever
its size, so looping is two to three orders of magnitude slower
than batching; see the sampler guide in the docs). This is the
batched form: the same times, many parameter sets, one dispatch.

``params_seq`` is either a sequence of TransitParams or a single
TransitParams whose scalar attributes are arrays of equal length.
Mixed circular and eccentric sets are fine: the transit-anchored
orbit degenerates exactly to the circular one at e = 0, so one
code path serves both.

For fitting with thousands of chains prefer ``elome.anvil``,
which owns the likelihood and the float32 conditioning as well.
```

### `TransitModel.light_curve_mx`

```python
light_curve_mx(params) -> mx.array
```

```text
Model flux as an MLX array that stays in the graph, for building
on in MLX -- differentiable in the parameters.

Any ``TransitParams`` field may be an ``mx.array`` scalar (t0, per,
rp, a, inc, ecc, w, fp, and ``u`` or its entries), and gradients
flow to every such field. Python numbers stay constants, folded on
the host exactly as ``light_curve`` folds them. With ``ecc`` a
Python number the result is ``light_curve``'s bit for bit when the
arrays are among t0, per, rp, fp, u and -- on an eccentric orbit
-- a, which enter the graph as they are. An array ``inc`` or
``w``, or ``a`` on a circular orbit, is combined in-graph in the
model dtype (b = a cos i, (k, h) = sqrt(e) (cos w, sin w)), which
on an fp32 model is within ~1 ulp of the host fold (see
``_model_eval``). Every field must be a scalar and ``u`` a flat
vector -- list, tuple, numpy or mx.array, or a list holding
mx.array scalars; a wrong shape raises before anything is built.

Returns the flux at the times given at construction, exposure-
averaged for ``integration="contact"``. With ``supersample_factor``
it is the raw supersampled grid -- reshape to (n_times, factor) and
average, as ``light_curve`` does.

Differentiable details:

* an array-valued ``ecc`` enters as (e, w) directly
  (``anchor_constants_ew``), so d/d(ecc) is finite and correct at
  e = 0 -- the one-sided derivative, since e >= 0 -- and d/dw is
  exactly 0 there. Out of [0, 1) it raises ValueError whenever the
  value can be read (eagerly, or under ``mx.grad``); when it is
  traced -- under ``mx.vmap`` or a caller's ``mx.compile`` -- it
  cannot raise, and instead the output and every gradient are NaN.
* a Python ``ecc`` keeps ``light_curve``'s own graph -- circular at
  e = 0, (k, h) above it -- so a fit that differentiates, say, only
  rp and t0 runs exactly as fast as ``light_curve``, fused kernel
  included. Only an array-valued ``ecc`` takes the (e, w) graph.
  For the quadratic law that forgoes the fused *model* kernel (see
  _get_compiled): measured 3-4x slower on an fp32 GPU model at
  2e6 points (3.0 vs 0.75-0.91 ms). The hybrid laws' photometry
  runs in their z-input kernel on every graph, this one included.
* ``u`` may be a list, a numpy array, or an mx.array vector.
* the contact-rule nodes move with the parameters, so a gradient
  is that of the quadrature actually evaluated.
* pass t0 as fp64 (a Python float or an fp64 array): an absolute
  BJD stored in fp32 has already lost its precision (0.25 d at
  2.45e6), before the model subtracts its reference time in fp64.
* under ``mx.grad`` MLX needs the CPU stream for *any* float64
  input. With an fp32 (GPU) model, differentiate float32 fields on
  the GPU; for an fp64 field such as an absolute t0, take the
  gradient inside ``with mx.stream(mx.cpu):`` (or use an fp64
  model, the default, which lives there anyway).

Precision: the graph is built on the model's own stream -- for the
default ``dtype=mx.float64`` that is the CPU, as MLX has no float64
on Metal. The result is a lazy fp64 array, so whatever you build on
it must stay on the CPU too: wrap your own ops (and ``mx.grad``) in
``with mx.stream(mx.cpu):``.
```

## The sampler API

Per-chain parameters in, per-chain light curves out, with analytic gradients. See {doc}`../guides/sampler-api`.

### `flux_dev_from_tau`

```python
flux_dev_from_tau(tau: mx.array, period, a, b, r, u1=None, u2=None, *, exp_time: float = 0.0, integration: str = 'contact', n_gl: int = 5, n_sub: int = 1, ld_basis: bool = False, secosw=None, sesinw=None, limb_dark: str = 'quadratic', u=None, f=None, theta=None, ring_in=None, ring_out=None, ring_f=None, ring_tau=None) -> mx.array
```

```text
F - 1 from time-since-mid-transit, with the exposure integrated
*inside* the kernel.

``tau`` is (n_chains, m) or (m,): each point's time relative to **its
own** mid-transit. That is the difference from ``make_quad_transit_flux``,
whose kernel derives the time from a linear ephemeris and therefore
returns a zero gradient for it -- a caller sampling per-epoch mid-times
(TTVs) cannot express its model that way. Here ``tau`` is an ordinary
differentiable input: build it however the parameterisation requires and
MLX chains the rest, which keeps this package out of the business of
knowing about TTVs or anyone's parameter vector.

The exposure rule runs per output point *in registers*, so the
sub-exposure axis never becomes an MLX array. A caller that expands it
instead pays ``n_sub`` times the memory in every forward intermediate
and in every gradient grid.

Args:
    tau: (n, m) or (m,) times since each point's own mid-transit
        (inferior conjunction), in the same units as ``period``.
        Its dtype is the computation's: float32 takes the kernel;
        anything else -- float64, a numpy float64 array, a Python
        sequence, float16, integers -- is float64 and takes the graph
        on the CPU stream (put there here; MLX has no fp64 on Metal).
        A parameter array of another dtype is cast to tau's. For
        ``mx.grad`` with respect to a float64 parameter, make the
        ``mx.grad`` call itself under ``mx.stream(mx.cpu)`` (MLX).
        Expected to lie within half a period of it -- that is what "its
        own" means.
    period, a, b, r, u1, u2: scalars or (n,), broadcast per chain as
        ``flux_dev_metal`` does. ``a`` is a/R*, ``b`` the impact
        parameter at conjunction, ``r`` = Rp/R*, ``u1``/``u2`` quadratic
        limb darkening.
    exp_time: exposure duration in tau's units; 0 means instantaneous
        (and forces ``integration="none"``).
    integration: ``"contact"`` -- Gauss-Legendre on the exposure window
        split at the four contact times, which Elómë's own numbers
        make strictly better per evaluation than supersampling (25 evals
        for 8.9e-8 against 101 for 1.7e-5 on a 29-minute exposure);
        ``"supersample"`` -- ``n_sub`` uniform nodes, batman's rule;
        ``"none"`` -- instantaneous.
    n_gl: Gauss-Legendre nodes per sub-interval. The window always has
        five sub-intervals, so the cost is 5 * n_gl evaluations.
    n_sub: number of nodes for ``"supersample"``.
    ld_basis: return the limb-darkening *basis* instead of one
        limb-darkened curve (off by default; see below). ``u1``/``u2``
        are then ignored and may be omitted.
    limb_dark, u: ``"quadratic"`` (the default, with ``u1``/``u2``), or
        a hybrid law ``"hybrid2" | "hybrid4" | "hybrid5"`` with ``u``
        its shape weights, ``(n_w,)`` shared or ``(n, n_w)`` per chain
        (see ``elome.hybrid``); same kernels' structure, no
        elliptic integrals. With ``ld_basis=True`` a hybrid law returns
        its (n, m, 1 + n_w) shape-basis columns B = [E0, T_1..T_n],
        and ``flux - 1 == (B @ c)/(N @ c)`` with ``c = (1, -w)``,
        ``N = hybrid.hybrid_norms(law)``.
    f, theta: an oblate planet (``elome.oblate``): projected
        flattening f = 1 - B/A and the sky angle of its long axis from
        the direction of motion at transit, scalars or (n,). ``r`` is
        then the area-equivalent radius sqrt(A B), with
        r <= (1 - f)^(3/2). Hybrid laws only. Omit both for a
        spherical planet (the default, whose paths they do not touch);
        theta defaults to 0 when f is given (sky frame and theta
        convention: ``oblate_tau``); the contacts are solved per side.
        fp32 data on the GPU takes the oblate Metal kernels
        (``metal_oblate``); fp64 the MLX graph on the CPU stream. In
        fp32, below f = 1e-5 a chain's value is the spherical forms'
        (the flattening's effect is under 4e-8), with d/df taken from
        the ellipse at f = 1e-5, so a fit can start at f = 0.
    ring_in, ring_out, ring_f, ring_tau: a ring in the planet's
        equatorial plane (``elome.rings``): inner and outer radii in
        units of ``r``, projected flattening ring_f = 1 - |cos i| of the
        ring, and normal optical depth (None or inf: opaque), scalars or
        (n,). Hybrid laws only; the planet is spherical unless f is
        given, and theta (defaulting to 0) orients the ring -- and the
        oblate planet, which shares it. The contact rule splits each
        exposure at the kinks inside it (``rings_tau``). fp32 data on
        the GPU takes the ring Metal kernels (``metal_rings``); fp64
        the MLX graph on the CPU stream.
    secosw, sesinw: (sqrt(e) cos w, sqrt(e) sin w), scalars or (n,).
        Omit both for a circular orbit (the default). Given, the orbit
        is the transit-anchored eccentric one (``anchored.py``), the
        same solve the model kernel runs: exact at e = 0, fp32-safe
        gradients as e -> 0, valid to e = 0.999. ``b`` stays the impact
        parameter at conjunction, a cos i (1 - e^2) / (1 + e sin w), so
        it reduces to the circular b at e = 0; circular and eccentric
        chains can share one batch.

Returns:
    (n, m) -- or (m,) for 1-D ``tau`` and no per-chain parameters -- of
    F - 1, exposure-averaged. Exactly 0 out of transit, as
    ``flux_dev_metal`` is.

    With ``ld_basis=True``: (n, m, 3) -- or (m, 3) under the same rule.
    ``B[..., j]`` is the exposure-averaged, *unnormalised* flux deficit
    of a star whose intensity is mu^j. It depends on geometry only, and
    for any quadratic law, with c = (1 - u1 - u2, u1 + 2 u2, -u2) and
    N = (pi, 2 pi / 3, pi / 2),

        flux_dev_from_tau(..., u1, u2) == (B @ c) / (N @ c)

    -- so a caller treating limb darkening as a linear block gets every
    law from one kernel launch. Costs about one scalar call.

Gradients flow in ``tau`` and in every parameter (``ld_basis`` drops
u1/u2 and takes a (..., 3) cotangent; ``secosw``/``sesinw`` add two).
fp64, the CPU stream, and machines without a usable Metal device take
the MLX graph path, which computes the same function.

For an eccentric orbit the contact split uses exact contact times
(``exposure.contact_offsets_anchored``: the linearised ones refined by
Newton through the anchored solve), so every split sits on its kink.
```

### `flux_dev_metal`

```python
flux_dev_metal(z: mx.array, r, u1=None, u2=None, *, ld_basis: bool = False, limb_dark: str = 'quadratic', u=None) -> mx.array
```

```text
F - 1 via the fused Metal kernels (fp32, GPU stream); silently
falls back to flux_dev_analytic for fp64, CPU streams, unsupported
layouts, or machines where the kernel probe fails.

The dtype of ``z`` is the dtype of the computation: float32 takes the
kernel; anything else (float64, a numpy float64 array, a Python
sequence, float16, integers) is float64 and takes the graph on the CPU
stream, put there here (MLX has no fp64 on Metal at all). A parameter
array of another dtype is cast to z's, on every route. For ``mx.grad``
with respect to a float64 parameter, make the ``mx.grad`` call itself
under ``mx.stream(mx.cpu)`` (an MLX rule; see ``fp64_on_cpu``).

With ``ld_basis=True`` it returns the limb-darkening basis instead:
shape ``z.shape + (3,)`` (with ``z`` broadcast over per-chain ``r``),
``B[..., j]`` the unnormalised deficit for intensity mu^j, so that for
any quadratic law ``flux_dev_metal(z, r, u1, u2) == (B @ c) / (N @ c)``
with c = (1 - u1 - u2, u1 + 2 u2, -u2) and N = (pi, 2 pi/3, pi/2).
``u1``/``u2`` are ignored there. See ``flux_dev_from_tau``.

``limb_dark="hybrid2" | "hybrid4" | "hybrid5"`` with ``u`` the shape
weights selects a hybrid law, as in ``flux_dev_from_tau``.
```

### `contact_offsets_oblate`

```python
contact_offsets_oblate(a, b, r, f, theta, k=None, h=None, ci=None)
```

```text
The four contact phases (ingress outer, ingress inner, egress inner,
egress outer) of an oblate planet, as offsets from mid-transit in
orbital phase (phi = 2 pi (t - t0) / P); ordered, detached.

a: a/R*; b: impact parameter at conjunction; r: area-equivalent radius;
f: flattening; theta: the long axis's sky angle [rad]; (k, h) =
(secosw, sesinw) for the transit-anchored eccentric orbit, with ci =
cos i (derived from (a, b, k, h) if omitted). Each argument a Python
number, a numpy array or an mx.array, broadcast together; the result
has their broadcast shape. Computed in float64 (on the CPU stream)
unless every array argument is float32. A missing contact collapses
onto a point inside the transit (the inner pair of a graze), or all
four onto one point (no transit).
```

### `ring_kinks`

```python
ring_kinks(a, b, r, f, theta, ring_in, ring_out, ring_f, k=None, h=None)
```

```text
The phases (offsets from mid-transit, phi = 2 pi (t - t0) / P) at
which a ringed planet's light curve has a kink -- an outline tangent to
the limb -- sorted, +inf in unused slots: shape (n, 24) for n parameter
sets broadcast from the arguments (Python numbers, numpy or mx arrays).
a: a/R*; b: impact parameter at conjunction; r, f, theta: the planet;
ring_in, ring_out, ring_f: the ring; (k, h) = (secosw, sesinw) for an
eccentric orbit. Float64 on the CPU stream unless every array argument
is float32.
```

### `metal_available`

```python
metal_available(reprobe: bool = False) -> bool
```

```text
Probe: can the fused kernel actually run on this machine?

The answer is cached for the process. A failure is not silent: it
warns once, with the exception, because every fp32 caller then takes
the MLX graph instead (correct, ~10x slower). ``reprobe=True`` forgets
the cached answer and probes again (after a transient device error,
say).
```

## Models and targets for anvil

Ready-made models and fitting problems for the anvil engine. See {doc}`../spherical/fitting`.

### `anvil.make_quad_transit_flux`

```python
make_quad_transit_flux(period_ref: float, analytic_vjp: bool = True, core: str = 'metal')
```

```text
Engine-contract batched model. period_ref is baked in as a plain
Python float (a numpy scalar here would silently force-evaluate the
graph mid-compile).

core selects the photometric implementation (identical forward math):
  "metal"    — fused Metal kernels on the fp32 GPU stream, silently
               falling back to "analytic" for fp64/CPU/unsupported
               machines (the default; anvil's fp64 verification path
               and CPU data generation ride the fallback);
  "analytic" — MLX graph forward + ALFM19 closed-form backward
               ("graph" is an alias, as for make_ecc_transit_flux);
  "autodiff" — pure reverse-mode autodiff (the reference).
analytic_vjp=False is a back-compat alias for core="autodiff".
```

### `anvil.make_ecc_transit_flux`

```python
make_ecc_transit_flux(period_ref: float, core: str = 'metal')
```

```text
Engine-contract batched eccentric model, v = (n_chains, 10) with
PARAM_NAMES_ECC and x = (2, m) epoch-centered times.

Eccentricity is sampled as (sqrt(e) cos w, sqrt(e) sin w), whose
e = 0 interior point a sampler genuinely visits; the transit-anchored
orbit keeps float32 gradients accurate there (see anchored.py). Pair
it with ``ecc_constraint_penalty`` — this function deliberately
returns finite flux for unphysical geometries, exactly as the
circular model does.
```

### `anvil.make_transit_target`

```python
make_transit_target(t, y, yerr, t0_guess, period_guess, eccentric: bool = False, bounds=None, policy=None, core: str = 'metal', strength: float = 1000000.0)
```

```text
Build an anvil fitting problem from REAL photometry.

``core`` is "metal" (default: fused fp32 kernels, falling back to the
analytic graph off the GPU), "analytic" (alias "graph") or "autodiff",
for circular and eccentric models alike.

This is the entry point for mission data (Kepler, TESS, ...). It owns
the conditioning that the float32 sampling path depends on, so a
caller never has to rediscover it:

* absolute times are reduced by a float64 ``t_ref`` and then turned
  into (per-orbit residual, orbit number) by ``epoch_center_times``
  -- raw BJD cannot survive float32 (0.25 d ulp at 2.457e6);
* flux is fit as ``y - 1`` so the graph carries O(depth) numbers;
* ``t0_guess``/``period_guess`` become the references the sampler
  perturbs around, and ``report_offset`` puts the reported values back
  on the original time system;
* for ``eccentric=True`` the joint-constraint barrier is attached.
  Elómë clamps every numerical hazard, so an unphysical geometry
  otherwise returns an ordinary finite log-likelihood and the chain
  samples an improper posterior in silence -- omitting the barrier is
  the single easiest way to get a wrong eccentric fit.

Args:
    t, y, yerr: photometry, any consistent time system; y normalized
        to ~1 out of transit.
    t0_guess, period_guess: references in the SAME system as ``t``.
        They need only be good to the width of the ``t0_off``/``p_off``
        boxes (0.5 d and 0.05 d by default).
    eccentric: 10-parameter model with (sqrt(e) cos w, sqrt(e) sin w)
        instead of the 8-parameter circular one.
    bounds: per-parameter (lo, hi) overrides on DEFAULT_BOUNDS. The
        defaults cap r at 0.5, b at 1.2 and a at 200; an occultor
        larger than the star (a white-dwarf host) needs them widened,
        e.g. ``{"r": (1.0, 12.0), "b": (0.0, 13.0), "a": (1.5, 1000.0)}``.
        The model takes any r > 0 (fp32 error grows ~ r^2; see the
        docs on occultors larger than the star).
    strength: barrier weight for the eccentric constraints.
```

### `anvil.TransitTarget`

```python
TransitTarget(target: object, transform: object, loglike: object, model_fn: object, x64: np.ndarray, y_fit: np.ndarray, yerr: np.ndarray, t_ref: float, t0_ref: float, period_ref: float, param_names: list, eccentric: bool) -> None
```

```text
A fitting problem over REAL data, ready for anvil.

``target`` is the TransformedLogDensity to sample; ``x64`` and
``y_fit`` are the conditioned inputs (epoch-centered times, flux minus
```


### `anvil.ecc_constraint_penalty`

```python
ecc_constraint_penalty(v, strength: float = 1000000.0, e_max: float = 0.999) -> mx.array
```

```text
Smooth barrier for the JOINT physical constraints that a box of
ParamSpecs cannot express (returns <= 0, exactly 0 when feasible).

  * periastron clearance   a (1 - e) > 1 + r
  * a real inclination     |cos i| <= 1
  * the eccentricity disc  secosw^2 + sesinw^2 <= e_max

Elómë clamps every numerical hazard, so an unphysical proposal
otherwise returns an ordinary *finite* log-likelihood and the chain
samples an improper posterior silently. A quadratic barrier is used
rather than a -inf wall because hard walls make HMC diverge.

The third term is what makes the barrier *escapable*. The model
projects (secosw, sesinw) radially onto the e_max disc, so outside it
the likelihood is exactly constant along the radial direction: a
chain thrown into the corners of the +/-0.95 box (where e_raw reaches
1.8) would sit on a plateau with no radial force pushing it back,
only the ParamSpec sigmoid Jacobian. Penalising the UNPROJECTED
e_raw restores a gradient that points inward.
```

### `anvil.PenalizedLogLike`

```python
PenalizedLogLike(base, penalty)
```

```text
``ChunkedGaussianLogLike`` plus a joint-constraint barrier.

The engine's ParamSpecs are per-parameter boxes, so constraints that
couple parameters have nowhere else to live; without this the chain
samples an improper posterior with no error message.
```

### `anvil.import_engine`

```python
import_engine()
```

```text
Import the anvil sampling engine.

Returns (engine_module, ChunkedGaussianLogLike). A missing engine
raises ImportError with the install command; an ``anvil`` that is
present but fails to import (a missing dependency of its own, or an
unrelated package of the same name) re-raises that error.
```

## Limb darkening

Laws, priors and the hybrid-law basis. See {doc}`../spherical/limb-darkening` and {doc}`hybrid-laws`.

### `q_to_u`

```python
q_to_u(q1: mx.array, q2: mx.array)
```

```text
(q1, q2) in [0,1]^2 -> (u1, u2), MLX ops (differentiable).

q1 is clamped away from 0 so sqrt has a finite gradient everywhere
(q1 -> 0 is the no-limb-darkening corner; the clamp is far below any
posterior mass in practice).
```

### `q_to_u_np`

```python
q_to_u_np(q1, q2)
```

```text
Float64 host-side replica of q_to_u.
```

### `u_to_q_np`

```python
u_to_q_np(u1, u2)
```

```text
Inverse map (host-side, for building initial states from u guesses).

q1 = (u1 + u2)^2, q2 = u1 / (2 (u1 + u2)). At the uniform disc,
u1 = u2 = 0, every q2 maps to the same u, and 0.5 is returned.
```

### `hybrid2_from_q`

```python
hybrid2_from_q(q1: mx.array, q2: mx.array, eps=None, law=None)
```

```text
(q1, q2) in [0,1]^2 -> (w1, w2) uniform on hybrid2's exact triangle,
MLX ops (differentiable): w = sqrt(q1) [(1 - q2) V_c + q2 V_l]. q1 is
clamped away from 0 as ``q_to_u`` does. For a custom hybrid2-type law,
pass it as ``law=`` so the triangle is the one for its pole.
```

### `hybrid2_from_q_np`

```python
hybrid2_from_q_np(q1, q2, eps=None, law=None)
```

```text
Float64 host-side replica of hybrid2_from_q, without its clamp:
exact on the edges of the square (no gradient is taken here).
```

### `hybrid2_to_q_np`

```python
hybrid2_to_q_np(w1, w2, eps=None, law=None)
```

```text
Inverse of hybrid2_from_q_np: solve w = s V_c + (s q2)(V_l - V_c).
```

### `hybrid4_from_q`

```python
hybrid4_from_q(q: mx.array) -> mx.array
```

```text
q (..., 4) in [0,1]^4 -> hybrid4 weights w (..., 4), uniform on its
curvature simplex -- exactly the profiles in its span that are
positive, monotonic, concave in mu^2 and of convex slope in mu^2, so
every q is such a profile and every such profile has a q (the analogue
of Kipping's q1, q2). The depth s = sum w = 1 - I(0) comes first,
s = q1^(1/4), then stick-breaking over the four shapes:

    w = s (1 - a,  a (1 - b),  a b (1 - q4),  a b q4),
    a = q2^(1/3),  b = q3^(1/2).

MLX ops; q clamped away from 0 for a finite gradient.
```

### `hybrid4_from_q_np`

```python
hybrid4_from_q_np(q)
```

```text
Float64 host-side replica of hybrid4_from_q, without its clamp:
exact on the faces of the cube, so tabulated q on a face give their
tabulated w (no gradient is taken here).
```

### `hybrid4_to_q_np`

```python
hybrid4_to_q_np(w)
```

```text
Inverse of hybrid4_from_q_np (host-side, for initial states):
q1 = s^4, q2 = (1 - w1/s)^3, q3 = (1 - w2/(s - w1))^2,
q4 = w4/(w3 + w4), s = sum w. A coordinate left undetermined (s = 0,
s = w1 or w3 + w4 = 0: every value maps to the same w) is 0.5.

w must lie in the curvature simplex (w_j >= 0, sum w_j <= 1): weights
outside it -- a profile convex in mu^2 somewhere, which hybrid4's
weights can describe but its prior excludes -- have no q, and raise.
```

### `simplex_from_q`

```python
simplex_from_q(q: mx.array) -> mx.array
```

```text
q (..., n) in [0,1]^n -> w (..., n) uniform on the simplex
{w_j >= 0, sum w_j <= 1} (hybrid5's prior, every point of which is a
physical profile; hybrid4's prior is ``hybrid4_from_q``), by stick-
breaking a flat Dirichlet: w_j = (1 - q_j^(1/(n-j))) prod_{i<j}
q_i^(1/(n-i)). MLX ops; q clamped away from 0 for a finite gradient.
```

### `simplex_from_q_np`

```python
simplex_from_q_np(q)
```

```text
Float64 host-side replica of simplex_from_q, without its clamp:
exact on the faces of the cube (no gradient is taken here).
```

### `q_from_simplex_np`

```python
q_from_simplex_np(w)
```

```text
Inverse of simplex_from_q_np (host-side, for initial states).

Once the stick is used up (sum w = 1 reached before the last weight),
the remaining q are undetermined -- every value maps to the same w --
and 0.5 is returned for them.
```

### `HybridLaw`

```python
HybridLaw(name: str, eps: tuple, shapes: tuple, mix: tuple | None = None) -> None
```

```text
A named law: its poles and its shape terms.

``shapes`` holds the even shape terms as (a0, a1, a2) coefficients over
the monomial columns (mu^0, mu^2, mu^4): (1, -1, 0) is 1 - mu^2,
(1, 0, -1) is 1 - mu^4, (1, -2, 1) is (1 - mu^2)^2. The pole shapes
Pi_eps follow, one per entry of ``eps``, in that order: together they
are the terms T = (even shapes..., pole shapes...).

``mix`` (optional, n_w x n_w, invertible, rows summing to 1) makes the
law's shapes the combinations S_k = sum_j mix[k][j] T_j, and its
weights refer to those:
I/I(1) = 1 - sum_k w_k S_k. Without it the shapes are T themselves.
hybrid4's ``mix`` is its curvature basis (``hybrid4_basis``).
```

### `HYBRID2`

```python
HYBRID2 = HybridLaw(name='hybrid2', eps=(0.36,), shapes=((1.0, -1.0, 0.0),), mix=None)
```


### `hybrid_norms`

```python
hybrid_norms(law) -> np.ndarray
```

```text
N = [pi, N_1..N_n] for the ``ld_basis`` contract
flux - 1 == (B @ c) / (N @ c), c = (1, -w). Float64, host-side.
```

### `hybrid4_basis`

```python
hybrid4_basis(eps) -> np.ndarray
```

```text
hybrid4's curvature basis for poles ``eps`` = (eps0, eps1): rows are
the shapes S1..S4 as combinations of T = (1 - mu^4, (1 - mu^2)^2,
Pi_eps0, Pi_eps1). With x = mu^2 and g = dI/dx, the weight simplex
w >= 0, sum w <= 1 in this basis is exactly the set of profiles in the
law's span with I >= 0, g >= 0, g' <= 0 and g'' >= 0 on [0, 1]:

    S1 = 1 - mu^2            (I = mu^2)
    S2 = (1 - mu^2)^2        (I = 1 - (1 - mu^2)^2)
    S3: I(0) = 0, g(1) = g'(1) = g''(1) = 0
    S4: I(0) = 0, g(1) = g'(1) = 0, g''(0) = 0
```

### `hybrid.ladder`

```python
ladder(K: int, alpha_eff: float = 1.0) -> tuple
```

```text
The analytic pole ladder eps_k = exp[(2 pi / sqrt alpha)
(sqrt(k + 1/2) - sqrt K)], k = 0..K-1 (alpha_eff = 1 for light curves),
as plain Python floats.
```

## Light curves from separations (float64 reference graphs)

Functions of the sky separation z (spherical) or the planet's centre in its principal frame (oblate, ringed). They follow MLX's broadcasting and type-promotion rules; see {doc}`../guides/gradients-and-precision`.

### `flux_dev`

```python
flux_dev(z: mx.array, r, u1, u2) -> mx.array
```

```text
F - 1 for a quadratic limb-darkened transit at separation(s) z.

F = sum_n g_n s_n / (pi (g0 + 2 g1/3)); writing s_n as deviations from
their unocculted values makes the numerator O(depth):

    F - 1 = (g0 s0d + g1 s1d + g2 s2d) / (pi (1 - u1/3 - u2/6))

All inputs broadcast; z drives the dtype.
```

### `flux_dev_analytic`

```python
flux_dev_analytic(z, r, u1, u2) -> mx.array
```

```text
flux_dev with an analytic backward pass. Same contract as
flux.flux_dev: z any array-like (float32 stays float32, anything else
is float64), parameters broadcastable and promoted as MLX does.
```

### `flux_dev_poly`

```python
flux_dev_poly(z: mx.array, r, u, n_max: int | None = None) -> mx.array
```

```text
F - 1 for an arbitrary-order polynomial law.

``u`` may be a host sequence (u_1..u_N) — then the u -> g transform
is folded into float64 constants — or an mx.array, in which case g
is built in-graph through the affine form of the same transform, so
the coefficients stay traced (batman-style updates, and gradients
with respect to the limb darkening).
```

### `flux_dev_hybrid`

```python
flux_dev_hybrid(z: mx.array, r, w, law) -> mx.array
```

```text
F - 1 for a hybrid law with shape weights ``w``.

``w`` may be a host sequence (folded into float64 constants), an
mx.array of shape (n_w,) -- traced, so gradients flow to the weights --
or (n_sets, n_w) batched, in which case each weight is a column that
broadcasts against z's leading (n_sets, ...) axes, exactly as
``flux_dev_poly`` handles its coefficients.
```

### `shape_cols`

```python
shape_cols(z: mx.array, r, law) -> mx.array
```

```text
The shape-basis columns B = [E0, S_1..S_n] (S_j the law's shapes:
for hybrid4 its curvature basis), stacked on a trailing axis: shape
z.shape + (1 + n_w,). Deviation form; 0 out of transit.
```

### `flux_dev_oblate`

```python
flux_dev_oblate(x0, y0, r, f, w, law) -> mx.array
```

```text
F - 1 for an oblate planet and a hybrid law with shape weights w
(a host sequence, (n_w,) or (..., n_w)); arguments as
``shape_cols_oblate``.
```

### `shape_cols_oblate`

```python
shape_cols_oblate(x0, y0, r, f, law) -> mx.array
```

```text
Shape-basis columns [E0, T_1..T_n] of an oblate planet, stacked on a
trailing axis -- the spherical path's ``hybrid.shape_cols`` layout and
``ld_basis`` contract (flux - 1 == (B @ c) / (N @ c), c = (1, -w),
N = hybrid_norms(law)). (x0, y0): centre in the principal frame
(``principal_frame``); r: area-equivalent radius; f: flattening, with
r <= (1 - f)^(3/2). y0, r and f arrays are cast to x0's dtype.
```

### `flux_dev_ring`

```python
flux_dev_ring(x0, y0, rp, f, ring_in, ring_out, ring_f, ring_tau, w, law) -> mx.array
```

```text
F - 1 for a ringed planet and a hybrid law with shape weights w (a
host sequence, (n_w,) or (..., n_w)); arguments as ``shape_cols_ring``.
```

### `shape_cols_ring`

```python
shape_cols_ring(x0, y0, rp, f, ring_in, ring_out, ring_f, ring_tau, law) -> mx.array
```

```text
Shape-basis columns [E0, S_1..S_n] of a ringed planet, stacked on a
trailing axis -- the ``ld_basis`` contract of the spherical and oblate
paths (flux - 1 == (B @ c) / (N @ c), c = (1, -w),
N = hybrid_norms(law)). Arguments as ``generator_cols_ring``; all are
cast to x0's dtype.
```

### `oblate.principal_frame`

```python
principal_frame(X, Y, theta)
```

```text
Sky position (X along the orbit, Y across) -> the planet centre in
the ellipse's principal frame, the long axis at sky angle theta from
the along-orbit direction: x0 = X cos theta + Y sin theta,
y0 = -X sin theta + Y cos theta.
```

```python
light_curve(z: mx.array, r, u1, u2) -> mx.array
```

```text
Absolute flux (1 out of transit) — standalone convenience.
```

```python
sn_dev(z: mx.array, r) -> tuple[mx.array, mx.array, mx.array]
```

```text
(s0 - pi, s1 - 2 pi/3, s2) broadcast over z and r.
```

```python
sn_dev_poly(z: mx.array, r, n_max: int) -> list
```

## Orbits and time

### `orbit.epoch_center_times`

```python
epoch_center_times(t_model: np.ndarray, t0_ref: float, period_ref: float) -> np.ndarray
```

```text
Float64 CPU preprocessing: times -> (2, m) [dt, orbit number].

dt = t - t0_ref - k * period_ref with k = round((t - t0_ref)/period_ref):
each datum's time relative to its own transit, plus which orbit it
belongs to (exact small integers): the (2, m) data contract of the
anvil model functions.
```

### `separation_keplerian`

```python
separation_keplerian(M: mx.array, e, a, inc, w, n_iter: int = 5)
```

```text
(z, front) for a Keplerian orbit, via the Cartesian-from-E tail.

M: mean anomaly from periastron (see mean_anomaly_offset_at_transit).
e, a (stellar radii), inc, w in radians — arrays or floats.

The true anomaly is never computed: with X = a (cos E - e) and
Y = a sqrt(1-e^2) sin E (orbital-plane Cartesians),
u = X cos w - Y sin w = r cos(w+f) and v = X sin w + Y cos w
= r sin(w+f) exactly, so z = sqrt(u^2 + (v cos i)^2) and the
front-side test is v > 0 (on the *unprojected* v — sign-safe for
any inclination). This form is uniformly better conditioned than
the previous conic tail: it has no 1 - sin^2(w+f) sin^2 i
cancellation near transit (which cost a ~1e-6 fp32 flux floor even
at e = 0) and no (1+e cos f) denominator collapse at near-apastron
transits (which reached 6e-3 flux error at e ~ 0.99); verified
exactly equivalent symbolically and to 4.5e-25 in 40-digit
arithmetic. The z floor guards only the backward pass's 1/z at the
exact-conjunction point (the forward sum of squares needs no clamp).

``front`` is True where a primary transit can occur (sin(w+f) > 0).
``n_iter`` is accepted for back-compat and unused (the Markley solve
is non-iterative).
```

### `separation_anchored`

```python
separation_anchored(phi, k, h, a, ci, eps: float = 1.1920929e-07, consts=None)
```

```text
(z, front) for an eccentric orbit, anchored at inferior conjunction.

phi = 2 pi (t - t0) / P (t0 = transit time), (k, h) the
(sqrt(e) cos w, sqrt(e) sin w) pair, a in stellar radii, ci = cos i.
Equivalent to ``kepler.separation_keplerian`` to round-off, and
conditioned so that fp32 *gradients* survive e -> 0. ``consts``, if
given, replaces (k, h) with an ``anchor_constants[_ew]`` tuple.
```

### `anchor_constants`

```python
anchor_constants(k, h)
```

```text
(k, h) = (sqrt(e) cos w, sqrt(e) sin w) -> anchored orbit constants.

Returns (e, ecw, esw, es, ec, B1, A2, B2). Every output is a smooth
function of (k, h) with a bounded derivative, including at e = 0 —
that is the whole point of the module. All of them are per-chain
scalars, so this runs in the MLX graph and its Jacobian rides
ordinary autodiff; only the per-point solve goes into a kernel.
```

### `kepler_E`

```python
kepler_E(M: mx.array, e, n_iter: int = 5) -> mx.array
```

```text
Eccentric anomaly E(M, e), Danby starter + fixed Halley steps.

Verification/back-compat path (the production solver is ``kepler``).
```

### `kepler.kepler`

```python
kepler(M: mx.array, e) -> tuple[mx.array, mx.array]
```

```text
(sin f, cos f) for mean anomaly M and eccentricity 0 <= e < 1.

Kept for RV-style uses and API compatibility; the transit-separation
path no longer goes through the true anomaly (see
``separation_keplerian``). Gradients via the implicit function
theorem, not by differentiating the solve.
```

### `kepler.kepler_E_sincos`

```python
kepler_E_sincos(M: mx.array, e) -> tuple[mx.array, mx.array]
```

```text
(sin E, cos E) with the E-level implicit gradient rule.

The transit-separation path stops at the eccentric anomaly: the
Cartesian tail in ``separation_keplerian`` needs only (sin E, cos E),
and the implicit rule here is simpler and better conditioned than the
f-level one (verified: the f-level factor degrades ~3x more in fp32
at near-apastron transit geometries).
```

### `trig.sincos`

```python
sincos(x: mx.array)
```

```text
(sin x, cos x), full working-precision in both dtypes.
```

## Special functions and transforms

### `cel`

```python
cel(kc: mx.array, p, a, b, n_iter: int | None = None) -> mx.array
```

```text
Batched cel(kc, p, a, b) for p > 0.

``kc`` must be an mx.array (its dtype drives the constants); p, a, b
may be arrays or Python scalars broadcastable against it. ``kc`` is
clamped to machine epsilon (the kc -> 0 limit of K diverges only
logarithmically, so the clamped value is accurate to ~eps*|log eps|)
and ``p`` to a tiny floor, making the masked-out branches of callers
NaN-free in both the forward and backward passes.
```

### `cel3`

```python
cel3(kc: mx.array, p, a1, b1, b2, b3, n_iter: int | None = None)
```

```text
Three cel integrals sharing one kc-recursion (Limbdark's vector cel).

Returns (cel(kc, p, a1, b1), cel(kc, 1, 1, b2), cel(kc, 1, 1, b3)).
The transit model uses this as (Pi-like, E(k), (E-(1-m)K)/m) — one
fixed-iteration loop instead of three. p > 0 required (clamped).
```

### `greens_transform_np`

```python
greens_transform_np(u: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
```

```text
u_1..u_N (any N >= 0) -> g_0..g_N, float64 host-side.

Port of the ALFM19 transform (as in jaxoplanet): prepend -1, binomial
change of basis (1-mu)^n -> mu^n with alternating signs, then the
downward g-recursion.
```

### `quad_g_coeffs`

```python
quad_g_coeffs(u1, u2)
```

```text
Quadratic-case g coefficients as MLX-safe expressions.

g0 = 1 - u1 - 1.5 u2,  g1 = u1 + 2 u2,  g2 = -0.25 u2
(verified against greens_transform_np). Works on mx.arrays or floats.
```

### `quad_norm`

```python
quad_norm(u1, u2)
```

```text
pi (g0 + 2 g1 / 3) = pi (1 - u1/3 - u2/6): the unocculted flux.
```
